h1: Exit options for brewery founders from sale to buyout
title: Exit options for brewery founders | Craft Beer School
desc: The ways brewery founders in India can exit: trade sale, sale to an operator, partner or management buyout, asset sale and closure, with what each route needs.
teaser: Nobody opens a brewery planning to leave. But how you might leave shapes how you should build it.
standfirst: Founders rarely think about exit until a partner wants out, an offer arrives or the numbers stop working. The options are clearer and the price better when the business was built with them in mind. Here is a plain map.
sections:
An exit is not only a sale for a big cheque. It is any way a founder stops owning or running the business: a partner leaving, a family taking over, a sale or a closure. Each route depends on decisions made years earlier, such as the legal structure, the founders' agreement, the quality of the books and whether the brewery can run without you.

Thinking about it early does not mean planning to leave. It means building something that someone else could buy.
Sale to a larger drinks company

A trade sale to a bigger brewer or drinks group is the exit people imagine. Buyers in this route usually want something specific: a brand with loyal drinkers, a production licence and capacity, a route to market in a state they find hard to enter or a team that can innovate.

A brewpub that is a great venue but has no brand beyond its address is less interesting to them. A brewery with packaged beer, distribution and a clear identity is more so. That is one reason the funding choices you make early matter: investors and trade buyers look for the same things.

Many brewpubs change hands to another hospitality operator who wants a running venue. The buyer values the location, the lease, the licences, the kit and the trade. Price usually follows verified earnings and the remaining lease term.

Licences are often the hard part. Liquor licences are generally tied to the entity and premises. Many states restrict transfer, so these deals are often done as a sale of the company's shares rather than its assets. Clean licences and records make the sale faster and the price firmer.

One founder buying out another is the most common exit we hear about. It goes smoothly when the founders' agreement already says how shares are valued, who has the first right to buy and how payment can be spread over time. Without those clauses it can become a long dispute. See brewery partner agreements for the clauses to put in on day one.

A management buyout, where the head brewer or general manager buys the business, can work when the team already runs it day to day. It usually needs the seller to accept part of the price over time, because managers rarely have the full amount upfront.

When a business is not viable, an orderly closure protects the founders far better than drifting. That means settling dues to staff, suppliers and the excise department, surrendering licences properly, handing back the premises and selling the equipment. Used brewing kit does sell, but at a discount. Buyers pay more for vessels with drawings, records and a history of good care.

Our guide to why breweries fail covers the warning signs worth acting on before closure becomes the only route.

• Books that are audited, current and match the excise records.
  • Licences and approvals in good standing, with no pending notices.
  • A lease with enough remaining term and a clause that allows a change of control.
  • Recipes, SOPs and quality records written down, not held in one person's head.
  • A team that can run the place for a month without the founder.

Each of these also makes the business better to own while you keep it.

Exits take longer than founders expect. Finding a buyer, due diligence, licence questions and landlord consent can stretch over many months. If a partner wants out in a hurry, or the cash is running low, the founder is negotiating from weakness. Starting the conversation while the business is healthy usually gets a better outcome, whatever the route.

Think too about what happens to the team. Staff who hear rumours of a sale start looking for other jobs. Decide early who needs to know and when.

Buyers usually value a running business on its sustainable earnings, then adjust for what they must spend to fix or grow it. Equipment value sets a floor, not a target. Founders often value the years and money they put in. Buyers value what the business earns next year. Knowing that gap before the first meeting saves a lot of disappointment.

Understanding how a buyer reads your P&L is part of running a brewery as a business. It is easier to learn long before the offer arrives.
faqs: What is the most common exit for a brewpub founder?
Partner buyouts and sales to another hospitality operator are common. Trade sales to larger drinks companies are rarer and favour breweries with a brand and distribution.
Can I sell a brewpub with its licences?
Many states restrict transferring liquor licences, so sales are often done by selling the company's shares. Rules vary by state, so take advice from a lawyer and licensing adviser.
Usually on sustainable earnings, adjusted for the cost of fixes or growth, with equipment value as a floor.
When should I think about exit?
When you set up the structure and founders' agreement. The clauses written then decide how smooth any later exit is.
